prompt.context: Our client is a grocery chain with 200 stores spread across the US. They have been enjoying good profits and great results, though in the last 2 years they have seen a slowdown in the growth of market share, and same store sales and profits have gone down. Wal-Mart opened a store exactly 2 years ago and 3 more in the past two years in the client's geography. The client also started, 5 years ago, to open smaller stores closer to where there is a high density of people.
prompt.question: We have been tasked to help the client overcome their current issues. What can be the reasons behind their low performance lately, and how should they address the competitive threats?

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of grocery items does Wal-Mart carry that our client also carries?
clarifying_info.a: Wal-Mart carries 75% of the grocery items our client has, at much lower prices.

clarifying_info.q: How does consumer perception compare between our client, Wal-Mart, and other competitors on pricing?
clarifying_info.a: Studies show consumers perceive our client's prices as higher than both Wal-Mart and another close competitor. In reality, prices are 20% higher than Wal-Mart and equal to the other competitor.

exhibits.title: Customer Perception by Factor
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing scores for Our Client, Competitor, and Wal-Mart across eight factors: Price, Promotions, Close to home, Variety of products, Fresh products, Organic products, Customer service, and Quickness. Scores range from 0 to 120.
exhibits.data: Factors on y-axis: Price, Promotions, Close to home, Variety of products, Fresh products, Organic products, Customer service, Quickness. Three bars per factor representing Competitor, WalMart, and Our client. Our client scores notably higher on Close to home and Fresh/Organic products; lower or comparable on Price and Promotions.

framework: Diagnose market share decline: revenue decline vs. cost increase
Revenue decline drivers: competition (Wal-Mart entry), consumer needs shift, pricing changes, assortment changes, promotion/loyalty changes
Cost increase drivers: higher unit costs from smaller new stores, price reductions, product mix shift to lower-margin items
Assess Wal-Mart threat and pricing image vs. competitors
Quantify impact of a proposed price reduction strategy
Use customer perception data to identify actionable differentiation levers
Form recommendation based on sustainable competitive advantages

questions.prompt: What are the reasons behind the client's low performance over the last 2 years?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will separate market share decline from profit decline. Market share could fall from customers spending less per visit, customers switching stores entirely, or the total market growing faster than the client captures. Profit could fall from revenue decline or cost increase. Key drivers: Wal-Mart's entry stealing consumers; unmet consumer needs (organic, services); pricing that is 20% above Wal-Mart; assortment or promotion changes; higher per-unit costs from smaller newer stores.

questions.prompt: How can the client address the threat of Wal-Mart and other competitors?
questions.guidance: Wal-Mart has only 4 stores vs. the client's 200, so the immediate threat is limited but the expansion risk is real. The client cannot compete on price with Wal-Mart. Strategy: conduct market research to find needs Wal-Mart cannot fulfill and build differentiation there. For the other competitor, address the pricing perception gap through a price sensitivity analysis — identify which products should carry low prices (high-visibility, price-sensitive SKUs) and which can sustain higher margins.

questions.prompt: The client decided to reduce prices by 15%. Based on the data provided, how many new stores must they open in the next 2 years to break even on the profit loss?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute current profit per store, then post-price-cut profit per store, find the per-store profit loss, aggregate over all 200 stores, and divide total profit loss by the new per-store profit to find the number of new stores needed. Candidate should also note that the number is infeasible given historical opening pace and the fact that new stores generate lower revenues.

math.setup: Sales/store = $40M; 200 stores; Profit margin = 30%; Price reduction = 15%. New sales/store = 85% * $40M. New profit/store = 30% * new sales. Total profit loss = (old profit/store - new profit/store) * 200. Stores needed = total profit loss / new profit per store.
math.answer: ~35 new stores needed; this is infeasible since only 40 stores were opened in the last 5 years and new stores generate below-average revenues, meaning the required number could be even higher.

questions.prompt: Based on the customer perception chart, what should the client do?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate identifies that 'Close to home' is the factor where the client outperforms competitors AND is presumably important to consumers (the client's strategy of opening smaller nearby stores supports this). Fresh and organic products are another advantage but are easily copied. The recommendation should focus marketing and investment on the defensible advantage (proximity/convenience) rather than the replicable ones.

brainstorming.prompt: What can be the reasons behind the client's low performance lately?

categories.name: Market share decline — revenue side
ideas: Customers spending less per visit due to competition
Customers switching entirely to Wal-Mart or other competitors
Overall market growing faster than client captures
Pricing perceived as too high, reducing traffic
Assortment changes causing loyal customers to shop elsewhere
Reduction in promotions or elimination of loyalty programs

categories.name: Profit decline — cost side
ideas: New smaller stores have higher costs per unit sold
Product mix shifting toward lower-margin items
Fixed cost dilution as same-store sales fall

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Wal-Mart entry with 75% product overlap at lower prices
Consumer perception of client as most expensive option
Wal-Mart's potential future expansion in the same geography
Other competitor with equal actual prices but better perceived value

categories.name: Consumer needs evolution
ideas: Shift in demographic or income profile of local customers

recommendation: Focus strategy on the 'Close to home' convenience advantage — it is the factor where the client leads and is difficult for Wal-Mart to replicate quickly
Accelerate the smaller-store format in high-density areas to deepen the proximity advantage
Build marketing and communications around convenience and fresh/organic assortment
Conduct price sensitivity analysis to selectively lower prices on high-visibility SKUs rather than a blanket 15% cut, which is infeasible to offset via new store openings
risks: Building a new brand image and consumer perception takes time; market share may continue declining in the short term
Fresh/organic advantage is easily copied by better-resourced competitors
New smaller stores carry higher per-unit costs, which pressure margins if revenues ramp slowly
Wal-Mart could accelerate store openings and erode proximity advantage in specific markets
next_steps: Commission price sensitivity study to identify the right SKUs for targeted price investment
Develop marketing campaign emphasizing convenience and fresh/local positioning
Evaluate pipeline of high-density locations for new smaller store openings
Track same-store sales trends by store vintage (pre-5-years vs. new) to monitor new-format performance
